item.title: The Diagonal of a Regular Pentagon
item.description: arXiv:2610.18903v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We demonstrate the well-known fact that the diagonal of a unit regular pentagon has length the golden ratio. While similar to other proofs, we provide a novel figure that we believe is particularly well-suited to achieve full understanding at a glance.
item.dc:creator: Dan McQuillan

item.title: Short Proofs for the Minimum Number of Determined Circles
item.description: arXiv:2610.18918v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present short proofs for the main parts of the recently completed solution of Erd\H{o}s Problem 506, which asks for the minimum number of distinct circles determined by a finite planar point set that is neither collinear nor concyclic. An inversion argument and a seven-point line lemma show that eight points determine at least $17$ circles, and an explicit configuration attains this bound. A single argument combining Melchior's inequality with Langer's incidence bound establishes the sharp formula for every $n\ge15$. The proofs give concise alternatives to longer arguments in the recent literature; the remaining finite cases are cited separately.
item.dc:creator: Stijn Cambie, Denis Paliy, Rafa{\l} Wrona

item.title: From a Student's Question to the Half-Derivative: A Constructivist Teaching Model - Part I
item.description: arXiv:2610.18932v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents a conceptual, cognitive-constructivist model for teaching the half-derivative. The model starts from a student's question and frames it as the problem of generalizing the familiar operation of differentiation. On a suitably chosen space of monomials, under the assumptions of linearity and of lowering the exponent by one half, the requirement that the operator applied twice give the ordinary derivative produces a recurrence for the coefficients. The freedom of normalization becomes visible, and an additional convention yields a formula compatible with the monomial rule of the Riemann-Liouville half-derivative. The domain of the operator and its relation to the Riemann-Liouville and Caputo operators are treated separately. The mathematical results rest on the author's earlier preprints; the contribution of this paper is their transformation into an instructional pathway organized in phases, with diagnostic questions, an analysis of typical errors, and comparative problems. The model is a design proposal: its effectiveness has not yet been established by systematic empirical research. The interactive Socratic implementation and the detailed diagnostics are the subject of Part II.
item.dc:creator: Davit Kapanadze

item.title: The grounded spirituality of mathematics
item.description: arXiv:2610.19216v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose that mathematics is done largely as a means of both coping with and celebrating our physicality in the natural world. Inspired by David Abram's "Becoming Animal", we suggest that -- in opposition to the popular image of an otherworldy Platonic realm-- the spiritual component of doing mathematics is grounded on and in the Earth. We explore this as a means of questioning the widespread adoption of AI in the workflows of research mathematics.
item.dc:creator: Tarik Aougab

item.title: An oral history of FPSAC
item.description: arXiv:2610.19236v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As its 40th anniversary nears, we present a history of the International Conference on Formal Power Series and Algebraic Combinatorics (FPSAC), through interviews with figures from its past, present, and future.
item.dc:creator: Sam Hopkins

item.title: Natural Geometry Based on the Rectilinear Plane
item.description: arXiv:2610.19253v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The aim of this note is to introduce natural geometry, in which the rectilinear plane is a primitive. This plane is admitted together with its rectitude, and its rectitude states that a Lambert quadrilateral has its fourth angle right. The fourth angle of a Lambert quadrilateral may be right, acute or obtuse, and this trichotomy distinguishes three planes. Starting from the rectitude, we prove the uniqueness of the parallel by a chain of neutral steps: the rectangle, the triangle whose angles sum to $\pi$, and Legendre's theorem \cite{legendre}, all borrowed from the classical literature. That uniqueness is equivalent to the fifth postulate, which we thus reach in Euclid's own wording: the equivalence is read in the natural direction, and it is not a derivation of the fifth postulate from the other four, since the independence of that postulate is not in question. In the rectilinear plane the parallels are characterised as exactly the images of a line under a point-reflection, and equivalently as the pairs of equidistant lines. The other two planes are then placed beside the rectilinear one, and the same definitions serve for all three.
item.dc:creator: Mohammed Berkani
